speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: As our built environment becomes denser and land development becomes more complex, URA has to apply a keener eye to guide development plans so as to safeguard the vibrancy and liveability of our urban space.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The amendments proposed in this Bill have three broad aims.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: I will go through these three in more detail.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Currently, URA may grant planning permission, subject to certain conditions and technical requirements that developers have to fulfil.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This allows URA to establish and advance good practices and design specifications that serve the public good.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The Bill amends the Act to supplement the conditions that URA can place on developers seeking planning permission.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: These additional conditions aim chiefly to create a more liveable and walkable cityscape, for example, through the provision of public spaces and pedestrian connections, and guiding the external appearance of buildings, like the night lighting of building facades.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The Bill also clarifies the persons who are required to comply with a planning condition.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Failure to comply with these conditions will amount to a breach of planning control, which is an offence.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This is to ensure that the public can continue to enjoy the pleasant environment and connectivity that were planned for at the outset, even if developments undergo a change of owners.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: That is the first limb, which is to enhance the planning levers.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Next, let me touch on the provisions in the Bill to strengthen the regulatory regime and there are several amendments in this regard.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The Bill introduces provisions relating to the responsibility of QPs, who are professionals, such as architects, engineers and surveyors.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Currently, developers applying for planning or conservation permission are not required by the Act to appoint a QP to prepare the plans and make submissions to URA, although in practice, most of them do so.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The Bill amends the Act to require that owners or developers appoint a QP to prepare these submissions to URA, in accordance with the Act's or URA's requirements.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The developer will similarly have to appoint a QP to supervise the development or works.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And this QP will have to notify URA if the works deviate from the approved plans or planning conditions, take reasonable steps to prevent deviations, and submit reports or declarations as required by URA.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This will minimise the need for subsequent rectification works, which can be costly for the developer or property owner.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: URA will be empowered to require the developer to submit as-built plans prepared by a land surveyor to facilitate cross-checking against plans which are initially approved.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: With QPs engaged throughout the key stages of the development process and held accountable for the discharge of their professional work, the new provisions in the Bill will ensure that planning controls and regulatory standards are observed in the course of development.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This serves to safeguard the quality of the environment and, at the same time, maintains good practices and overall standards in the industry.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Minor works and simple applications may reasonably be exempted from these requirements.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Another aspect of strengthening the regulatory regime is to have enhanced powers of investigation which this Bill will provide for.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: In particular, where URA officers believe that persons might have knowledge of a violation, the officers will be empowered to require these persons to attend interviews and question them.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Apart from verbally examining witnesses and recording statements, URA will also be able to require the production of information or documents relevant to the violation, and to take video evidence on site.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Where necessary, officers will be able to effect forced entry to carry out their investigation.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This broad set of provisions is aligned with the enforcement powers of other agencies.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: There are also stricter penalties for unauthorised development or works because where violations are uncovered, the Bill puts in place a series of penalties for the offences under the Act.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The current level of fines is too low to serve as a strong deterrent against unlawful activity or conduct.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: For example, URA has increasingly encountered unauthorised dormitories, including some repeat offenders.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The penalties for demolishing a conserved building must also be enhanced as any unauthorised demolition will result in an irrevocable loss of our built heritage.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: With that in mind, the Bill will put in place stricter penalties.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The Bill also ensures that culpable parties are held to account by making it clear that permitting unauthorised development or works is an offence.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, owners will have to exercise due diligence on their tenants and contractors.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The Bill will make explicit the lawful boundaries pertaining to residential rental and subletting.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Private residential properties should not be used for other purposes without planning approval, as there is a need to safeguard the living environment of residents in the neighbourhood.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This cap does not apply to families, as the amendment expressly excludes persons who are related, along with their domestic helpers and caregivers.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This set of regulations will apply only to private developments and will not apply to the Housing and Development Board (HDB) flats, which come under a separate set of controls managed by HDB.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: I have covered the second broad component of provisions which relate to strengthening the regulatory regime.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Thirdly, there are a series of things we are doing in this Bill to streamline the administration of the Act.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: First, it allows URA to give preliminary advice to developers and property owners or their QPs on their proposals prior to submission of their development applications.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This would be an added service for developers or their QP to seek a preliminary indication from URA, at an earlier stage, as to whether their proposal satisfies the relevant regulations or guidelines.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The Bill provides for this additional service that URA will provide.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Second, the Act currently allows URA to defer the payment of the development charge for charity organisations; and the Bill amends the Act to allow the deferral of this charge to be carried on to the next property owner, where the Minister approves of the deferral, for example, where the next owner is also a charitable organisation.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: It will allow URA to be more effective in regulating planning violations and ensuring that our physical living environment continues to be of a high quality.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: URA has consulted with stakeholders and professional institutes, including the Real Estate Developers' Association of Singapore (REDAS) and the Singapore Institute of Architects (SIA), on the amendments to the Act.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: They have provided useful feedback, which have been taken into consideration in the drafting of this Bill.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: With that, Mdm Speaker, I beg to move.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: It was said that one day, this old man walked past a rundown knick-knack store and spotted an old ceramic teapot on display, his eyes gleamed and a grin spread across his face.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: He walked in briskly and said to the young man sitting rather boredly behind the counter and said: "Young man, I will give you $1,000 for that teapot in the window." The young salesman replied: "That old dusty teapot?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Why would you want it?" Without explaining, the old man told him, "Wrap it up, I will be back in an hour with the cash," before leaving the shop.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The young salesman thought to himself that it was incredible that someone would pay such an amount, but thinking perhaps the old man saw something of value, he quickly brushed the teapot and washed it out, wiping it so well that a shine returned.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: When the old man returned, the young man said, "Sir, I have polished it up and it is almost like new.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I think it is now worth $2,000!" In horror and almost immediately crestfallen, the old man said, "My friend, sadly, it is now worthless, for its worth was in the well-seasoned pot blackened by decades of tea-brewing.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Now that it is new and polished, it is worthless to me." Mr Deputy Speaker, our built environment is one that is more than functional.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: It plays a huge role in affecting a community, a nation, both psychologically as well as culturally.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: It marks where we have come from and where we are headed.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Therefore, the Planning Bill has played an important role in ensuring that the built environment that we choose to live in, and not just one that we have no choice but to try to live in, is one that is dynamic and yet true to our history and our culture.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Like that teapot, old may not always mean worthless and new may not always be valuable.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Even as the Bill aims to create a delightful cityscape and a more walkable city, I hope that we take a moment to also ponder at what we have lost or might lose in the search of progress, in search of orderliness.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Many of our heritage districts are wonderful to behold, picturesque, but to put it bluntly, they may be all but in name.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: They are often sterile, clean, clinical representations of their past; sometimes commercialised to the point of soullessness.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Perhaps the grime is a mark of character of a building, of a district, that in our urge to be utilitarian and for progress, we lose some of what makes us, us.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Take the case in point of the Ellison Building at the corner of Bukit Timah and Selegie.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: It is perhaps a bit ironic that we have in one Ministry gazetted it as a heritage asset but, in another, has had to take the hard decision to demolish it for the public good.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In my recent work trips to the United Kingdom and Taiwan, private enterprise and some government initiatives have returned life to old derelict structures, imbuing them not just with a new vitality, but also one that continues with tradition and one that is exciting to a new audience, welcomed not just by locals but tourists alike.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: What more can we do so that our children and future generations of Singaporeans do not become poorer for the heritage that we lose?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Who does not delight in a beautiful cityscape skyline?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Most major cities have one that they are proud of.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We have one that we should be proud of, too − a marriage of old and new − a story of our nation's development in one picture-perfect photo.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: But I hasten to ask, who is going to pay for it all?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Under the new URA guidelines and requirements, new buildings will be required to conform to certain design aesthetics.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Who would not agree that it would be nice to light up the skies every night?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: But just as we go about urging Singaporeans to conserve energy and utilities, lighting up the night sky may end up burning a fire in the wallet.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: So, greater clarity in this area on expenditure and control of expenditure, and use of utilities would be useful.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: With regard to the provision of public areas and pedestrian connections, I spent a working visit to Hong Kong late last year traversing the city centre and the civic district without once emerging into the direct sunlight or the light year-end drizzle.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: From skylinks to underground passages, you could cover a large portion of the financial and civic district with ease.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Aiming towards this would certainly benefit Singaporeans and visitors alike, considering our very equatorial climate and fondness for the rain.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: If a building, especially older strata title ones, holds out from renovation or rebuilding, can the Ministry compel the building owners to make earlier provisions for connectivity, especially when the buildings serve as the middle of the sandwich between two newer developments that have already made provisions?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In Hong Kong, I am given to understand that a large portion of the connected buildings are owned or managed by the same developer and, of course, it makes sense for them to have the connectivity planned early.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In previous cases in Singapore, we have also seen new buildings which were required under the guidelines to provide linkages, but abutting buildings refusing to link up, resulting in gaps for pedestrians.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Will this be sufficiently addressed by the amendments, and will abutting buildings also be compelled to make good on bridging the gaps?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In terms of a peaceful living environment, one of the areas that perhaps gained most interest on infringements and enhanced powers of investigations provided to URA, has to do with how we keep the peace in our living environment, especially when there are units that have a higher proportion of subtenants.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Many are understandably concerned about their neighbouring units being overcrowded, and their safe and peaceful living environment is made less so by strangers coming in and out or changing ever so often.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I have a number of clarifications to seek from the Minister.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This is well and good, but I am unable at the moment to reconcile the numbers with the guidelines that are set out separately by HDB.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: So, if a 4-room flat can have nine subtenants, the new limitations on private property, some of which would be bigger, seem to be out of sync.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I am not advocating for the fact that we should increase the number of allowed subtenants to nine, but the question remains whether HDB guidelines should also correspondingly be revised to reflect this new reality in the Planning (Amendment) Bill.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: But I understand that the URA guidelines have been in place since 2009 as guidelines.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Why has it taken eight years for it to be legislated?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Is it because of an increase in number of violations or number of complaints that we are, therefore, required to now legislate this?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This legislation will also make a rather popular travel arrangement seemingly legal.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I am sure many of us who travel are familiar with the AirBnB concept or even couch-surfing.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I know that the Ministry is currently studying and drafting legislation, or propose legislation on regulations on new markets, such as AirBnB.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: But by codifying the amendments to the Planning (Amendment) Bill now, does it run counter to what is being planned for any new legislation in the future?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: How will the URA, therefore, police current AirBnB listings now that they will all be considered legal subletting?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Notwithstanding the questions I have raised, I give my support to the Bill.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Many of my residents will appreciate this change, which states categorically that it will be illegal for owners to lease out their properties to short-term renters, unless they have a special permit.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I have received numerous negative feedback from my constituents about the disamenity caused by such visitors.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: They have expressed their concerns about compromised security in their estates, the loss of privacy and the occasional disturbances.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Despite URA's guidelines forbidding such rentals, thousands of condominium and room listings can be found on rental portals, such as Airbnb, Roomorama, PandaBed and HomeAway.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Many of them can be rented for durations as short as one night.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Many of my residents have complained to me that the problem lies in the lack of follow up or enforcement.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Usually, the Police and URA have the details, including the exact addresses and profiles of visitors.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: These beleaguered neighbours submit all the information required and hope for swift action to be taken.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Unfortunately, the transient strangers continue to stream in.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Due to the presence of these visitors, residents feel less safe and are perpetually on their guard.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Barely half a century has passed since we implemented a proper framework, and our housing has been transformed from dirty slums and vulnerable kampungs to the beautiful high-rise buildings we have today.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I welcome the changes to reduce the number of people to sublet to not more than six in private housing, and I am sure it will decrease the disamenities faced by the affected residents.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: After all, home is a place for us to rest after a long day.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: My question is: why not extend this to HDB flats?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: An overcrowded apartment can be very noisy and a constant source of stress and irritation to the neighbours.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Residents have come to me with feedback about their neighbours' rowdy tenants.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Furthermore, some of these tenants would leave footwear and other belongings along the common corridor, which is not only unsightly but inconveniences the other neighbours.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: During my recent house visit, a resident complained to me about a neighbour's sublet flat.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: She said that the tenants even spit and smoke at the lift lobby and loiter along the corridors.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Quite often, it is because there are a lot of people in that flat.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: On a related note, there needs to be stronger enforcement against home owners who rent out their homes as temporary accommodation to overseas visitors.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Currently, HDB and URA regulations dictate that renting a whole unit or individual rooms is only allowed for long-term stays of six months or more.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: This is a long-standing rule that applies to both private property and HDB housing.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: However, judging by the number of rentals still available online, this generally seems to be enforced only when people complain.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: In the meantime, many residents have to endure the ill effects.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I have residents complaining to me about tourists on their floor, moving luggage in and out at odd hours of the day, disturbing their rest.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Instead of having this "one-eye open, one-eye closed" policy, we should state our stand clearly and take enforcement action immediately.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Why wait until there are complaints for action to be taken?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Trends like Airbnb rentals are rising, but I think we need to look into how to balance the two.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Some countries have designated certain apartment buildings for rental to foreigners.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: This way, locals know of the policy before they decide whether to buy that apartment.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: In Japan, hosts have to obey local laws set by Japan's Hotel Business Act which governs overnight stays.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Just like these countries, we should look deeper into alternative ways to deal with this new trend.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Meanwhile, everybody should stick to the law, and I hope that our relevant agencies will take action.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Next, moving on to structural issues, I would like to suggest extending this Planning Bill to include two things.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: First, imposing on the developer to build covered linkways from the condominium or executive condominium (EC) to the nearest bus stop.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I think many of our new HDB Build-To-Order (BTO) flats have a covered linkway to the nearest bus stop but not the new condominium or new EC.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: And later on, when the residents shift in, they will ask for this new covered linkway which is very difficult for us to implement after that.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Second, facilitating linkages between buildings, like what Hong Kong's Planning Department does with their Urban Design Guidelines.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: This will make walking in the city more pleasant, with better connectivity.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: For those who have been to Hong Kong, I am sure you enjoy shopping and walking in Hong Kong much more than in Singapore because you can walk from one building to another building without walking under the sun because the buildings are all connected.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I know that it is not easy, but we must start somewhere.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: On another point, I also wish this Bill could give more assistance to those who live in landed property and have difficulty obtaining access to do up their house, for example, plastering their external walls.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I think all of us know that it is good practice to plaster the external walls so that you do not get water seepage.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: But I have seen cases from time to time, residents telling me that they really have problems in getting access because of the objections from neighbours and then when they go to URA or the Building and Construction Authority (BCA), no one can help them.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I hope that with this Planning amendment, we can look into cases like this.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: And please allow me to summarise in Mandarin.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: (In Mandarin):   Mr Deputy Speaker, our home should be our harbour.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: However, the neighbour's tenants can sometimes disturb the peace of other residents greatly.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: This amendment provides that private housing can only house a maximum of six tenants.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: This will help to improve the situation faced by some residents.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: However, currently, 4-room or larger HDB flats can house a maximum of nine tenants.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Tenants in HDB flats live in even closer proximity to their neighbours.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Therefore, can the Government consider reducing the maximum number of people who can stay in an HDB flat to six as well?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: On another note, short-term rental is becoming more and more popular.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Although current rules dictate that no residence can be rented out for less than six months, there are plenty of such short-term listings online.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Is the Government only able to act after people complain?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Rather than adopting this "one eye open, one eye closed" approach, why do we not explore other solutions?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: After all, the Government has always been encouraging Singaporeans to take public transportation.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: However, in my view there are some points for further review which I would like to share with the House.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: For smaller units, this could result in overcrowding.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: For bigger units, it is an unnecessary constraint which would deprive owners of additional rental income.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Casting a stronger focus on safety and hygiene, the Ministry could look into specifying available square footage per occupant and the level of amenities, such as toilets and bathrooms, provided on a per person basis.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Such specifications will set the basic standards for living conditions and prevent owners from subdividing their units further to create more rooms.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This will help to enhance not only the well-being of the occupants but of the neighbours as well.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: With many rooms and residences in Singapore now being offered on Airbnb, it would be advisable to provide this group of owners with more clarity on whether they should withdraw their listings to avoid running afoul of the law.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Another area of concern is the proposed section 12A.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The owner of a property must satisfy, on a balance of probabilities, that he has taken "all reasonable precautions" to prevent the contravention by the tenant or contractor, or demonstrate "due diligence" but could not have prevented the contravention by the tenant or contractors.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The challenge here is what constitutes "all reasonable precautions" or "exercise due diligence".

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: These are grey areas that will only be decided if the case goes before a Court.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The owner may think that he has taken "all reasonable precautions" but the authority may view otherwise.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Some of us may recall that many years ago, a number of landlords were charged for harbouring illegal immigrants.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The law did not spell out the requirements and duty of the owners but merely stated the requirement of "due diligence".

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The Courts took pain in those years to interpret what constituted "due diligence".

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The result then was that the bulk of the cases were slapped with convictions rather than acquittal.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Subsequently, in 2004 and 2007, section 57 of the Immigration Act was amended twice, and new sub-sections were inserted to explain the kind of acts that the house owners must carry out to avoid prosecution.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Similar ambiguity, if applied to section 12A, could cause undue stress on owners and result in unnecessary legal issues and costs.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This is especially so if the owners are elderly, physically impaired or illiterate.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In some cases, the owners have assigned power of attorney to a third party to lease to tenants and, in the event of a contravention of section 12A, does it mean that the owners would still be taken to task?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It is the same whether you are in Singapore, Germany or the United Kingdom (UK).

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Today, with the popularity of Airbnb, a Singaporean can, if there are no rules in place, wake up one day and find himself being stared at by, say, someone from another country staying next door and a new one every other week, month or so.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I am sure it would raise his/her suspicions and he/she or would be asking himself or herself, "What and who is this?" And this is what will happen if we do not control property owners who turn their premises into a hostel or use it for Airbnb activities.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: With these rules in place, it will be easier to carry out enforcement against property owners who use their premises for prohibited activities.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Thanks to mainstream and social media, it is widely known that renting out homes for short-term stays is, in fact, forbidden.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But this is not stopping Singaporean Airbnb listings from popping up ever so frequently.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I think it is important that the Ministry takes a clear stand on it or it will be assumed that the regulation is a paper tiger.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In this market where some flat owners are hard-pressed to get tenants, some of them have resorted to renting out their units to short-term travellers.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Will this deter old buildings from being redeveloped?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In my constituency, there are quite a number of condominiums, for example, which may be affected by these changes in the Bill and also in the city-centre as well.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: With so many different designs for buildings in Singapore, both residential and commercial, we need to have some coordination in their appearance.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: What can be done to ensure that there is some cohesion in the design, unless we are open to a bit of differentiation and chaos and that whether there is good connectivity for pedestrians to move from one to another and what it impacts as well?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: With the rules clearly spelt out for enforcement purpose, it will positively support enforcement personnel to conduct their duties, hold the owners responsible and render early intervention to some local issues without wastage of our public resources.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: The amendment on subletting of a property to an excessive number of unrelated persons in this Bill, I feel, is a welcome move.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Not only does it assist enforcers to conduct their checks, it also prevents situations where safety is a concern and the relevant authorities were unable to gain access into properties to take the necessary actions.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Such stories are not unheard of during my house visits and Meet-the-People sessions.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Here, I would like to raise a few areas which I felt the Ministry should further consider, as enhanced enforcement powers may not suffice under some conditions.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: But, with regard to concerns on overcrowding and safety, the size of a HDB flat generally poses more of these challenges, given its limited space compared to a landed property.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: I have received numerous feedback from residents living in HDB flats of suspected units housing more than the specified number of tenants allowed under the current guidelines.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Second, during my house visits, I have encountered units that are occupied by elderly couples or those living alone with a domestic helper.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: These people are understandably sometimes reluctant to provide access of their premises to the authorities due to uncertainty and lack of trust in strangers.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: The case in point is not a concern of excessive subletting but on other areas, like the need for the authorities to inspect the presence of mosquito breeding, building structure conformance and so on.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Should the Bill be passed, how can the authorities assist these elderly persons to ensure that they are safeguarded through a process to provide access and not fear of being penalised for not complying on the first instance?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Third, while the current focus is about non-compliance being the responsibility of home owners and developers of the property, we may have neglected the role that the property agents play in such transactions.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: In cases where excessive subletting occurs, what is the probability that rental agreements were made without the assistance of a property agent and that the agent was unaware of tenancy conditions in the said property breaching the stipulated guidelines?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: And if proven so, will the property agent be equally liable for committing the offence as the home owner?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: I would urge the Ministry to consider having some of the enforcement terms as compulsory clauses within the rental agreements and the contractual agreements between the owner and the property agents.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Tougher measures have to be taken against those who violate and possibly imposing a debarment period in which the owners are not allowed to rent their property.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Enforcement is often viewed as an essential process for checks on compliance when the rules or guidelines are in place.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: However, when it is not explicitly written in legal terms, it is usually difficult for the enforcers to take any recourse against those who offend.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: The requirement to appoint QPs is absolutely necessary as the process of compliance during planning, construction and the final building structure has tremendous implication on safety.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Be it for conservation, commercial or residential purpose, safety is an aspect that we cannot compromise.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: If the buildings were not constructed in accordance with approved plans, the cost of rectification will be huge and, at times, irreplaceable.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: It is likely that many owners are layman when it comes to building design and materials used, and they are ignorant of the building requirements and the terminologies.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Many have dreams of what they hope their final design would be for their prized possession.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: However, many cannot articulate these details nor have any idea how the process may be like until they embark on some of these projects.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Some errant developers may present false claims of their capabilities and hard sell before the contract is signed.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: This was exactly the issue that one of my residents faced recently.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Like most owners, they had entrusted the project solely to the contractors.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Being a first-time owner of a landed property, they were unsure of the processes involved.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Unknowingly, their trust in the contractor, whom they thought would have the architect and the QP appointed to supervise the project, turned out to be a nightmare for them.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Often, owners would not have sight of the new developments in the building rules and are technically challenged to understand the construction progress or even check against what materials had been used.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: This is even more difficult when the structures are embedded or concealed.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: On this note, Mr Deputy Speaker, I rise in support of the Bill and look forward to the inclusion of these new clauses and that legalising the terms would help our enforcers to carry out their duties more efficiently, giving rise to safer buildings and developments in our city state.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I will focus my speech on the short-term rentals, and I note that it is already illegal to lease a home for less than six months in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: However, what we are doing in this Bill is codifying this URA subletting guideline, and I have concerns about this.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My concern is that this Bill might be passed too hastily.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I stress that these statements were published not more than a year ago.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: While this Bill might be passed, can the Minister clarify if his Ministry will be studying this issue further, will he be conducting more public consultations and do a further review on this?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The sharing economy, while disruptive, is here to stay.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We have witnessed this with Uber and Grab.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Likewise, home-sharing concepts, like Airbnb and PandaBed, are here to stay.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Passing the law to combat the real or perceived negativities of the home-sharing economy diverges from the approach that was taken against similarly disruptive entrants in Uber and Grab.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We are also ignoring the popularity of such "disruptive" home-sharing concepts, especially with the younger generation, and how this might ultimately also affect our tourism industry.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: At last year's National Day Rally, the Prime Minister noted that there are two ways to respond to disruption: (i) to close Singapore off and try to stop people from using the new technology, or (ii) embrace change and let the disruption happen, but help the incumbents adapt.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The Prime Minister said that old models are not working.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: New models are coming in thick and fast, and we have to adjust and keep up because of technology and globalisation, and the disruption will happen over and over again, relentlessly.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I hope that we do not close Singapore off to the home-sharing economy and stop Singaporeans and tourists from using such platforms in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I believe that we should embrace this disruption and explore ways to help all stakeholders adapt to the new normal.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Given that home-sharing platforms have many users and customers, does URA have enough manpower to undertake full enforcement measures in the first place?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: How many enforcement officers does URA have to enforce this?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Following the passing of this Bill, will it require all the listings ‒ all 6,000 or so, as my colleague Er Dr Lee Bee Wah has stated ‒ on these home-sharing platforms to be removed?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: And, lastly, has URA conducted research on how other countries have regulated the home-sharing concept?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister share if we are considering following some of these regulations?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Lastly, Sir, I would like to thank the Minister for introducing a custodial sentence for repeat offenders of permitting unauthorised development and subdivision.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This is necessary because recalcitrance at the expense of damaging Singapore's heritage and identity should never be tolerated.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I am heartened by the addition of section 24B to the Act, which adds another layer of protection to conservation areas in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I note that in discharging their duties, QPs are required to notify URA of any contravention or non-compliance with any provision, condition, requirement or plans in relation to this Act.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Could the Minister consider adding a time factor into this obligation, to notify "without delay", "immediately" or "as soon as practicable"?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I believe that the earlier the non-compliance is reported, the higher the chance that we could prevent or mitigate problems that may arise from that non-compliance.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Deputy Speaker, thanks for allowing me to participate in this debate.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I support the Bill but have some suggestions for the Minister's consideration.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The intention is to deal with the recurrent problem of subletting to too many tenants, resulting in overcrowding.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, as properties vary greatly in terms of size and configuration, may I recommend that the Ministry limit the number of tenants based on the sizes and types of rooms of the residences?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Currently, a Singapore Citizen is allowed to sublet the entire HDB flat after fulfilling the minimum occupation period.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The maximum number of sub-tenants allowed in each flat is based on flat type.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Private properties should be subjected to similar caps as well.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Thirdly, I would like to request for greater protection for tenants.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Does the Ministry keep track of how many such cases of complaints have occurred in the past five years?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Will the Ministry implement measures to deter such cases from recurring?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In addition, often, owners and their tenants have disputes over whether the deposits should be returned, and some owners keep the deposits at the end of the leases without valid reasons.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Would the Ministry consider setting up a Government-approved lease deposit account in which landlords are required to place their tenants' deposits?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This will help enhance protection for tenants and facilitate recovery of their deposits.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I would also like to ask how many cases there have been of tenants subletting to other tenants in the last five years.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: What are the typical profiles of such tenants and what actions have been taken against them?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: If they are foreigners, would the Ministry consider banning them from working and living in Singapore?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In addition, would the Minister share how many cases of disputes between neighbours involving Singapore residents and foreign tenants there were in the past five years?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Does the Ministry keep track of the nature of the disputes so that we will be able to formulate better preventive measures?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: That is the very intention of this Bill and URA will, where meaningful to provide for such connectivity, require developers to do so for new developments.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: For existing developments, the provisions in the Bill do not envisage an imposition on the existing buildings.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But should the property owners of these existing buildings choose to redevelop their properties or choose to make additions and alterations in their properties, and they have to seek URA's planning permission to do so, then that would be an opportune time for URA to impose these new conditions.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I think many Members would be supportive of these additions and these provisions to impose conditions on developers to enhance connectivity and building standards.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But there were some Members, in particular, Mr Saktiandi Supaat and Mr Alex Yam, who were concerned about the cost impact and how this will impact on the building and perhaps even on residents.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: In addition, URA will not require every development to provide public space or connectivity.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: It will do so judiciously and where it is meaningful to do so.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: These requirements will only be applied, for example, to strategically located sites in key areas or where there is provision or if it is meaningful to provide for connectivity.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, there is a way to balance the different requirements, and we will be mindful that even as we impose these provisions, they do not lead to a significant escalation of costs.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah asked a separate matter about access to neighbouring property to execute works, such as the plastering of walls.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I understand this is a concern very often found in private residential areas.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: It is really not so much a planning issue but a matter of resolving disputes between two property owners.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: URA cannot override the property owner's rights, but it will help to facilitate mediation between neighbours to resolve issues, if necessary.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: That is my first reply on the broad area of planning levers.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Next, let me touch on the points that Members have raised on the responsibilities of home owners, and potentially even extending that to other stakeholders like property agents.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And here, there was also a mix of views.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Ms Joan Pereira and Miss Cheryl Chan wanted to be sure that we can take suitable action against home owners and property agents responsible for offences, but I believe Mr Chong Kee Hiong sought assurance that home owners would not be burdened unnecessarily by the amendments.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And again, it is about striking the right balance.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Where any property has been misused or unauthorised works done, URA will ensure that culpable parties are all taken to task, whether for committing or abetting the offence.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: For home owners who do not reside in or are not in Singapore, URA will obtain the owner's home address from ICA and the Inland Revenue Authority of Singapore (IRAS), and they still have to answer the charges if there is a violation of the rules.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I think this is in response to Ms Joan Pereira's question.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: If there is evidence to show that a property agent is complicit in an infringement, they will be referred to the Council of Estate Agents (CEA), who will sanction them accordingly.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I think that is something that Miss Cheryl Chan had asked about.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: When it comes to enforcement, URA will, if necessary, beef up its enforcement capability and resources but it will also work with other agencies, for example, ICA, the Singapore Police Force (SPF), the Ministry of Manpower (MOM), the Singapore Civil Defence Force (SCDF) and the National Environment Agency (NEA), as Mr Gan Thiam Poh had suggested, to share information on any suspected cases of unauthorised use of private property and take the necessary enforcement actions.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Miss Cheryl Chan shared the concerns of elderly home owners who may be taken to task for not assisting enforcement checks.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: They will, first, identify themselves when there is a need to inspect premises and also explain the intentions of their visit.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Officers will not force the occupants to allow them to enter, unless repeated requests to enter have been denied or they assess that critical evidence will be lost if they cannot gain access in a timely manner.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Several Members, including Mr Alex Yam and Mr Chong Kee Hiong, asked about the precautions that building owners or property owners would have to take and what is deemed to be appropriate due diligence.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I think it is very difficult and not so practical to draw out all the different scenarios and due diligence steps that have to be taken in legislation itself, but I would just like to assure Members that URA would carefully assess the culpability of persons involved, given all the facts available on each particular case at hand, and ensure that owners who have no part in directing the violation are not unduly penalised.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: URA will not make egregious demands on owners, and whether or not due diligence has been exercised will be assessed reasonably.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Another section of the provisions in the amendment Bill for which there were some comments was on the role of QPs.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Miss Cheryl Chan asked about the professionalism of QPs.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The Board of Architects and the Professional Engineers Board oversee the professional development of architects and engineers, respectively.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: For instance, in order to renew their practising certificates annually, both architects and engineers have to meet "continuing professional development" requirements to update their competencies.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: All registered architects and engineers are listed on their relevant board's website.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, if there is any question or doubt about whether or not this is a QP, you can look at the website of the relevant board.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The professions have their regulatory regimes in place to ensure that those listed are competent to discharge their duties lawfully.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The Board of Architects and the Professional Engineers Board will not hesitate to take disciplinary action against registered professionals who fall foul of regulations.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Depending on the severity, the QP may be fined, suspended or deregistered.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: This Bill also gives URA more powers to charge QPs in Court, if necessary, for instance, if they had provided false declarations.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Mr Louis Ng suggested that a time factor be added to QPs' obligation to notify URA of contravention or non-compliance of requirements under the Act.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Other than notifying the authorities, the Bill already requires the QP to "take all reasonable steps to immediately stop or cease the contravention".

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: This is ultimately what matters, as conditions at a construction site are constantly changing.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, I believe that the provisions in the Bill are sufficient to meet the Member's concern in this regard.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: It was, again, one of the topics here that has attracted quite a number of views.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah suggested that the flat cap of six tenants be now imposed on HDB flats, so that it is consistent between private and public housing.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: In HDB flats, there are predictable typologies of design and layout, and a simple set of rules can be based on the number of rooms.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Unlike HDB flats, private housing comes in wide-ranging varieties and configurations.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: It would be hard to formulate a rule that could capture all the variations along the scale of private residential housing, from shoebox flats to bungalows.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We have considered this, but we think that a complicated tiered cap may be confusing for the public and may result in uncertainty for those who want to rent or sublet legitimately.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: In fact, the cap of six persons was the original cap that used to be in place before.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But this cap was raised to eight in 2008, and it was due specifically to ease a crunch in the housing supply for workers.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: As for reviewing the HDB limits, I think that is a separate matter.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: It is not within the remit of the Planning Act because the HDB controls are regulated separately, but we would be happy to do the review of the occupancy cap for HDB flats on a separate basis.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I must first clarify that the amendments in this Bill do not amount to a change of policy.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: There is already an existing URA guideline against any short-term accommodation of less than six months in private residences.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: A breach of these guidelines can be considered a material change of use, which will then be deemed an offence under the Planning Act.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: This remains the case under the amendments to the Act and the same penalties apply.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: In fact, URA had undertaken public consultation on this matter of short-term accommodation in 2015, and in its focus group discussions with stakeholders, such as Neighbourhood Committees and managing agents of private residential developments, there was also strong endorsement of the need to preserve the privacy and sanctity valued by the vast majority of home owners.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Likewise, several Members just now − Mr Saktiandi Supaat, Ms Joan Pereria, Er Dr Lee Bee Wah and Mr Alex Yam, among others − shared their constituents' experiences and expressed strong support for these rules, and also, in fact, strong support for enforcement.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I know Mr Louis Ng felt that this perhaps was done in haste, but I also heard Er Dr Lee Bee Wah who asked why we took so long to put this in place.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: On balance, we will have to enforce the current rules, which we have been doing and will continue to do.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: These are issues that we take seriously and we should enforce the current rules, as we are already doing, and make sure that the issue does not worsen further.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The amendments to the Act will enable URA to do so.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: In terms of enforcement, URA will continue with its current enforcement approach on errant home owners, which means that when you look at advertising on home-sharing or rental websites, that, in itself, is not an offence and it is not regulated under the Planning Act, because these listings typically do not indicate the tenure of lease.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: On the basis of the listing on the site, it is not possible to take action.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But as a first step, what URA will do is to work with the MCST of the development which have units with online listings and they will put up notifications to the residents in that development, so that the residents are aware of the rules on short-term accommodation.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Then, if the short-term rentals persist and cause disamenities for other home owners, URA will step in to enforce.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I agree with Ms Joan Pereira that MCSTs can also do their part.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Under the Building Maintenance and Strata Management Act (BMSMA), MCSTs have oversight of common property.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: For example, they can pass their own by-laws to manage the use and enjoyment of their common property through screening and record-keeping.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: They can also pass by-laws to register the details of all visitors.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Indeed, in its earlier consultation, URA had received feedback from a number of respondents, including home owners, that there was scope to reduce the minimum period of rental in a private residence.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, URA is studying this carefully, and will consider a possible reduction in the minimum rental timeframe.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: URA will consider whether there can be scope to reduce this timeframe.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But whatever adjustments we may make to this minimum period, it is clear that it will not accommodate residential homes that are being put up for daily rental, which is meaning to say, even if we were to reduce from six months to three months, for example, this would not accommodate residential homes that are converted to daily rental of rooms which are operating very much more like hotels.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: In fact, such premises which are rented out on a daily basis really ought to be regulated more like hotels rather than residential homes, and they should be subjected to relevant licensing and conditions to ensure proper standards.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: That was also the feedback that URA had received from various stakeholders, and we also note that many cities in Asia and around the world are likewise regulating short-term home-sharing platforms in a similar way to hotels and serviced apartments.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, in response to the point made by Mr Louis Ng, we had, indeed, studied the models used by other cities.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Indeed, for many of them, where it comes to short-term stays that are operating very much more like daily rentals the way a hotel or a service apartment would, the city municipal governments are taking actions and regulating them like hotels or serviced apartments.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: New residential sites can be sold with such an approved use, allowing flexibility for short-term rentals.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: For existing residential buildings, they would then require planning permission for change of use, and this would be subject to a set of guidelines which URA is looking into.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: What I have described just now, these proposed measures are separate from the amendments that are being tabled today.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: What I have described just now with this option of creating a new use class for private residences to engage in short-term rentals, can be done without changes to the Act.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: URA is studying them, and they will provide more details soon for further engagement and consultation with the stakeholders.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I shared what we are thinking about because there is obviously strong interest from Members, and I thought I should clarify our approach and current thinking on this matter, and also explain that we do see a role for home-sharing platforms to continue operating in Singapore so long as they are properly regulated and so long as there is a level playing field between them and similar entities that provide short-term rentals like hotels and service apartments.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I agree that the sharing economy is here to stay; this is a point that several Members had said.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We will allow a space in our city for such platforms to exist.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The amendments in this Bill will strengthen URA's ability to safeguard and enhance the vibrancy and liveability of our urban space.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah
text: On the part of the access for plastering, if you think that mediation can solve the problem, then we do not have residents coming to us, complaining or sharing with us the problems that they face.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah
text: So, I thought this is the right time to put in place a requirement.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah
text: Actually, if the house owners know that, at the end of the day, they have no choice but still have to give them the access, maybe the problem can be resolved much easier.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah
text: Because today, they know that your URA, your BCA, all have got no teeth.

text: But we are not just leaving this alone.
